Accelerate database changes, reduce failures, and enforce governance across your pipelines. *This is one section of our complete 12-part guide to* *CI/CD for databases - get your copy**.*. Database changes must be handled safely and with minimal human intervention to maintain their steady flow through the CI/CD pipeline. By creating automated checks throughout the pipeline, you can ensure changes occur safely within the technical and business policies governing application and database development in your organization. Governance of databases and their change management processes is critical to achieve consistency, quality, and security while maintaining speed and efficiency. The trick with setting up governance for database change workflows in the CI/CD pipeline is to know where your delivery process needs them and where it does not. That said, there are two common types of database governance that will almost certainly factor into your effort: Path Markers and Problem Stoppers. Problem Stoppers serve as safety points that ensure that if new changes deviate from the standards, they will be blocked from proceeding farther down the pipeline, made visible for the team to address, and will not be allowed to continue until remediated. In CI/CD terms, Path Markers will take the form of well-defined automation points or the handoff points between automation systems. Examples of CI/CD Path Markers include:. * This is what the CI system will do with your change. * Using Liquibase Policy (Quality) Checks to ensure the safety and compliance of your changes against your rules. Database governance places protective constructs along your CI/CD pipeline to ensure a smooth and safe path from change creation to eventual deployment into production. By carefully considering how to guide changes through a reliable workflow and redirect them when they get off course, this governance ensures trustworthy pipelines and  ensures that when trouble inevitably happens, it does not get out of hand. results.title: CQRS in Practice: Handling Data Consistency and Eventual Consistency | Reintech media
results.content: # CQRS in Practice: Handling Data Consistency and Eventual Consistency. Command Query Responsibility Segregation (CQRS) is an architectural pattern that treats the actions of reading and writing data as fundamentally different operations, warranting separate models. By segregating commands (writes) from queries (reads), developers can optimize each operation's performance and scale them independently. However, one of the complexities introduced by this approach is dealing with data consistency, particularly eventual consistency. ## Dealing with Data Consistency. In a CQRS system, the write model typically leads to changes in the read model through a process known as event sourcing. This process involves capturing all changes to an application state as a sequence of events, which can then be processed asynchronously to update the read model. Given that updates to the read model are not instantaneous, this introduces eventual consistency. To manage eventual consistency, developers need a well-thought-out strategy that caters to the domain's specific requirements. * **Retry Policies:** Implement retry policies for handling transient failures during event processing. A typical pattern is to use an event bus or message queue to dispatch events to handlers responsible for updating the read model. ## Synchronizing Write and Read Models. To ensure consistency between write and read models, developers can use several strategies:. * **Saga Pattern:** A series of related domain events that are handled in a sequence, ensuring a consistent state across bounded contexts. * **Immediate Consistency:** An option where critical flows require instant read-after-write consistency. This can be achieved by updating the read model directly within the command handling transaction. * **Background Process:** Running a background service that synchronizes the write and read models at regular intervals. ## Eventual Consistency in Practice. The essence of eventual consistency is that all systems will become consistent over time. To manage eventual consistency effectively, monitoring and logging mechanisms should be put in place. CQRS provides clear benefits in terms of scalability and separation of concerns but requires careful consideration around data consistency models. By employing strategies like versioning, event handling best practices, and monitoring techniques, developers can confidently implement CQRS without compromising data integrity. results.title: Eventual Consistency in Distributed Systems: A Framework Analysis of CRDT Based Resolution, Vector Clock Synchronization, and Partition Mechanisms for Scalable Multi-Node Data Consistency | by Kalyan Chakravarthy | Medium
results.content: # Eventual Consistency in Distributed Systems: A Framework Analysis of CRDT Based Resolution, Vector Clock Synchronization, and Partition Mechanisms for Scalable Multi-Node Data Consistency. The challenge of maintaining data consistency across distributed systems stems from fundamental computer science principles. Eventual consistency represents a specific consistency model within the spectrum of data consistency guarantees. Unlike strong consistency models that enforce immediate synchronization across all nodes, eventual consistency guarantees that if no new updates are made to a given data item, eventually all accesses will return the last updated value. This model aligns with the BASE (Basically Available, Soft state, Eventually consistent) principles that contrast with the traditional ACID (Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability) properties of database transactions. Eventual consistency provides a practical solution by relaxing the consistency requirements while still maintaining reasonable data accuracy. While eventual consistency introduces complexity in application logic, it provides the scalability and availability required for modern internet services.

results.title: Architecting for Scale [Part 2] : Eventual Consistency and Handling Large-Scale Data | by Abhishek Kumar | Medium
results.content: # Architecting for Scale [Part 2] : Eventual Consistency and Handling Large-Scale Data. Eventual consistency is a consistency model used in distributed computing to achieve high availability that informally guarantees that, if no new updates are made to a given data item, eventually all accesses to that item will return the last updated value. Under eventual consistency, when data is written to one part of the system, it can take some time before it becomes visible to all other parts of the system. It is a consistency model used in distributed systems where updates to data are propagated to all nodes in a distributed network over time, rather than instantaneously.
